title: Week 28 Check-In · By the Great Horn Spoon!
description: This week you read Chapters 10 to 12. You practiced transitions and introductory phrases, the roots fort and val/valid, the endings -ity, -ment and -ness, how character choices build a theme, two themes in one poem, and a literary response. Show what you know.

questions.label: Identification
questions.text: Which transition shows a contrast between two ideas?

questions.label: Punctuate
questions.text: Rewrite the sentence with correct punctuation.
questions.excerpt: The road agents held the stage nevertheless Praiseworthy stayed calm.
questions.key: The road agents held the stage; nevertheless, Praiseworthy stayed calm. (semicolon before, comma after)
questions.from: 28.1 and 28.3 Grammar rule; Oct 11 QTI Q3
questions.status: kept from the Oct 11 quiz (made-up sentence, not a book line)

questions.label: Introductory Phrase
questions.text: Which sentence puts the comma in the right place?
options: After a long climb, the stage reached the top of the hill.
After a long climb the stage, reached the top of the hill.
After, a long climb the stage reached the top of the hill.
After a long climb the stage reached, the top of the hill.
questions.status: new (introductory phrases; the scope's second half)

questions.label: Root
questions.text: Which word contains the root val (strong, worth)?
questions.status: fixed (the page keyed prevail, whose root is spelled vail; festival is a look-alike decoy)

questions.label: Root Meaning
questions.text: What does fortitude mean, based on its root?
options: Strength and courage in hard times
The act of making something stronger

questions.label: Context Clues
questions.text: Read the line from Chapter 11. What does exasperation mean here?
questions.excerpt: Praiseworthy’s patience was a marvel — and an exasperation.
questions.status: new (vocabulary in context; replaces 'use valor in a sentence')

questions.label: Build the Noun
questions.text: Turn each word into an abstract noun and name the ending you used: valid, achieve, dark.

questions.label: Base Word Change
questions.text: In which word does the base word change its spelling when the ending is added?
questions.status: new (spelling change at the join; replaces a sentence-writing item)

questions.label: Key Detail
questions.text: How does Praiseworthy keep the gold dust safe during the robbery in Chapter 10?
options: He pulls off his glove carefully but casually, and the dust stays in the fingers.
He hides it inside his hat.
He drops it in the dirt so the outlaws miss it.
He gives it to Jack to hide.

questions.label: Character Choice
questions.text: Why does Praiseworthy stop trying to correct the miners’ story? What does this choice show about him? Answer in 2–3 sentences.
questions.key: The miners won't listen and prefer the tall tale; he decides to go along (even adds to it), which shows he can bend, has a sense of humor, and is adapting to life in the diggings.
questions.status: kept (1 point; the passage is now printed above it)

questions.label: Read Like a Writer
questions.text: In Chapter 11, Jack forces down coffee he can hardly swallow. What does this choice show?
options: He wants to belong and keep the name Jamoka Jack.
He is trying to stay awake.
He wants to make Pitch-pine Billy angry.
questions.status: new (the scope's Read Like a Writer focus: theme through character choices)

questions.label: Poetry
questions.text: Tennyson’s eagle clasps the crag and falls like a thunderbolt, but he also lives in lonely lands. What does this show?
options: A poem can carry more than one theme at once.
The eagle is afraid of falling.
The poem is only about the weather.

questions.label: Literary Response Opening
questions.text: Write the opening of your literary response (3–5 sentences). Include the book title, the author’s name, your theme claim, and one character’s choice as evidence. Use one transition and one abstract noun (-ity, -ment or -ness), and underline the abstract noun.
questions.key: Title + Sid Fleischman + a theme claim (an idea, not a topic) + one character choice + a transition + an underlined abstract noun.
questions.status: changed (adds the character-choice focus; now 1 point)

passage.title: Reading passage (Chapter 12)
passage.text: Praiseworthy shouldered the pick. He gave up trying to explain. It seemed to him that every man in the diggings became hard of hearing when he wanted to, and he’d had enough of that for one day. If they preferred a tall tale to the facts, let them have it.
passage.cite: Sid Fleischman, By the Great Horn Spoon!, Chapter 12
